The worked examples and questions use km/h and hours at a level above Stage 4, so they should be replaced with a simpler Stage 4 example using whole-number distances and times.
The point should not rely on the gradient terminology or on the returning-to-start line, which goes beyond the single idea of reading speed as distance divided by time.

draft.title: Distance-time graphs
card: A distance-time graph has time across the bottom and distance from the start up the side. Each point shows how far something has travelled at that time.
A steeper line means a faster speed. A flat line means no movement, because the distance is not changing.
To find a speed, divide a distance by the time it took: speed \(=\) distance \(\div\) time. Use any two points on a straight part of the line.
Ava rides 10 km in the first 2 hours, then stops for 1 hour. Her speed is \(10 \div 2 = 5\) km/h, then 0 km/h while the line is flat.

4.alt: A distance-time graph for Ava. The line rises from \((0, 0)\) to \((2, 10)\), then is flat from \((2, 10)\) to \((3, 10)\).

draft.remember: Steeper means faster, flat means stopped, and speed is distance divided by time.

a.q: On a distance-time graph, what does a flat line show?
opts: The object is moving at a steady speed
The object is going back to the start
a.why: A flat line means the distance does not change while time passes, so the object is not moving. A slow object would still show a line that rises, just not steeply.
a.clue: What happens to the distance as time goes on?

b.q: Leo walks 6 km in 2 hours, rests, then walks 6 km more in 1 hour. Which part of the graph is steeper, and what is the speed there?
b.why: The first part is \(6 \div 2 = 3\) km/h. The second part is \(6 \div 1 = 6\) km/h. The distance is the same, but the second part takes less time, so it is faster and steeper.
b.clue: Divide each distance by its own time and compare.

problems.detail: The first line says the vertical axis is 'distance from the start', then says each point shows 'how far something has travelled'. These differ when an object turns back: distance travelled never decreases, but distance from the start does. One consistent phrase, such as 'distance from the start', would avoid confusion.
